cards.explanation: The answer is the Most Holy Place, friends. The man measures the room next to the inner sanctuary at twenty cubits long and twenty cubits wide, and then he says to Ezekiel, "This is the Most Holy Place." (Ezekiel 41:4) Notice it's a perfect square. I like a tidy room.

The answer is the table that is before the LORD, friends. The wooden altar is three cubits high and two cubits square, and the man tells Ezekiel, "This is the table that is before the LORD." (Ezekiel 41:22) Altar and table in one verse, so if your head does a little spin, that's fair. I think a table is a good place to be when you're before the LORD.

The answer is priests, friends. The man says these are the holy chambers "…where the priests who approach the LORD will eat the most holy offerings." (Ezekiel 42:13) So the chambers are for priests, and the offerings are eaten right there. Grain offerings, sin offerings and guilt offerings are all named in that verse.

The answer is True, friends. The man says the priests will place the most holy offerings there, "…for the place is holy." (Ezekiel 42:13) The grain offerings, sin offerings and guilt offerings are all named. The text gives the reason right in the verse, so I don't have to guess.

The answer is False, friends. The man says the priests "…must not go out into the outer court until they have left behind the garments in which they minister, for these are holy." (Ezekiel 42:14) So they can't just stroll out wearing them. The garments stay, and other clothes go on.

The answer is because those garments are holy, friends. The man says the priests must leave the garments behind "…for these are holy." (Ezekiel 42:14) The reason is right there in the verse. Holy garments stay in the holy place.

The answer is people, friends. The man says the priests "…are to put on other clothes before they approach the places that are for the people." (Ezekiel 42:14) So there's a change of clothes between the holy area and the people. Simple as that.

The answer is to separate the holy from the common, friends. After all that measuring, the text says the wall was there "…to separate the holy from the common." (Ezekiel 42:20) Five hundred cubits long and five hundred cubits wide, with a wall all the way around. The text tells us what the wall is for, so no guessing needed.
